issues.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction to determine whether land is or is not village common land when that question is part of the dispute.
material_facts: The appellants sued for a declaration that they owned land in their possession and that the village body had no interest in it.
The trial court transferred the suit after finding that the dispute concerned whether the land was excluded from the statutory definition of village common land.
That finding was not challenged before the High Court or in the special-leave petition.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had no jurisdiction to try the suit insofar as deciding it required determining whether the land was village common land.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(a)(i) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, as amended, bars civil courts from entertaining or adjudicating whether land or other immovable property is or is not shamilat deh. The court relied on the unchallenged finding that this question formed part of the dispute. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.civil_suit_over_village_common_land: A plaintiff brings a civil suit concerning land claimed to be village common land.
predicates.dispute_includes_common_land_status: The dispute requires deciding whether the land is or is not village common land.
predicates.trial_finding_on_status_issue_unchalleng: The trial court finds that the dispute includes the land's common-land status, and the parties do not challenge that finding in later proceedings.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerning village common land requires a decision on the land's status, and the trial court's finding that it does is left unchallenged, the civil court lacks jurisdiction to determine that status.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide an ownership claim to village common land when deciding it would determine whether the land or an interest in it vests in the village body.
material_facts: The appellants claimed ownership of the land in their possession and argued that they had acquired title by adverse possession.
They argued that the land's status as village common land was admitted and that only their title claim remained to be decided.
The Court considered that argument on the assumption that the land was village common land and concluded that deciding title would determine whether the land vested in the village body.
issues.conclusion: Even if the land's status as village common land was not in dispute, the civil court had no jurisdiction to decide the appellants' title claim because that decision would determine whether the land vested in the village body.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(a)(ii) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, as amended, bars civil courts from entertaining or adjudicating whether land or any right, title or interest in it vests or does not vest under the Act. The Court treated the asserted acquisition of title to village common land as raising that vesting question. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.civil_suit_over_village_common_land: A plaintiff brings a civil suit asserting an interest in land claimed to be village common land.
predicates.land_is_village_common_land: The land in dispute is treated as village common land.
predicates.ownership_claim_requires_deciding_vestin: Deciding the plaintiff's ownership claim would determine whether the land or an interest in it vests in the village body.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerns village common land and resolving the ownership claim would determine whether the land or an interest in it vests in the village body, the civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide that claim.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to a former provision requiring transfer of pending suits need not be decided after that provision has been omitted with retrospective effect.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the provision under which their pending civil suit had been transferred to a revenue authority.
While the appeal was pending, legislation omitted that transfer provision with retrospective effect.
The Court concluded that the constitutional validity of the omitted provision no longer needed consideration and addressed the civil court's jurisdiction under the amended law instead.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not decide the constitutional validity of the former transfer provision because it had been omitted with retrospective effect.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the retrospective omission of the former transfer provision as making its constitutional validity unnecessary to decide in the appeal. It then considered jurisdiction under the amended section 13, including clauses (a)(i) and (a)(ii), of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_challenges_transfer_order: A party appeals an order transferring a pending civil suit under a statutory transfer provision.
predicates.transfer_provision_omitted_retroactively: The transfer provision is omitted with retrospective effect while the appeal is pending.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a transfer order and the transfer provision is omitted retrospectively during the appeal, the court does not decide the provision's constitutional validity.
